sourceTitle: The Convenient Virtue of the Perfect Consumer
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independently authored EN/C2 review-comprehension test draft. External linguistic and didactic audit pending.

tabs.title: Evidence and evaluation
tabs.description: Evaluate what the reviewer supports and questions.

tabs.title: Critical transfer
tabs.description: Apply the review's argument in new contexts.

questions.q: What does the overflowing bin outside the film screening demonstrate?
choices: The documentary secretly opposes reusable containers.
A festival cannot function without disposable cups.
The audience has misunderstood the teenager's personal achievement.
Celebrating an individual example can leave institutional practices outside the story.
questions.explanation: The applause directed at a virtuous teenager sits beside an unexamined institutional source of waste.

questions.q: Why does the author refuse to dismiss the venue's contradiction simply as hypocrisy?
choices: The audience has no responsibility for the setting of a screening.
A moral accusation would ignore constraints and the documentary's selective treatment of responsibility.
The venue has already solved all of its logistical problems.
The film-makers cannot be expected to know how waste is collected.
questions.explanation: The writer prefers understanding systems and narrative framing to the easy satisfaction of moral blame.

questions.q: How does a 'perfect-consumer narrative' make a causal claim without stating one explicitly?
choices: It centres visible individual acts while excluding less cinematic institutional arrangements.
It demonstrates that reusable flasks are always environmentally superior.
It identifies all the organisations involved in waste processing.
It shows that choices are unrelated to larger environmental systems.
questions.explanation: The film's selection of protagonists and omissions implies individual moral behaviour is the complete cause of outcomes.

questions.q: What is the significance of the school installing water fountains after a student campaign?
choices: Public infrastructure is independent of voting, protest or habits.
The teenager's flask is environmentally neutral in every context.
Personal actions and institutional provision can influence one another.
Student campaigns succeed only when schools remove individual choices.
questions.explanation: The example illustrates interaction between personal practice and collective systems.

questions.q: Why does the writer complicate the claim that a metal flask is necessarily responsible?
choices: A reusable product is harmful whenever it is lost.
A disposable cup always has a smaller environmental impact.
Metal is too expensive for most educational institutions.
Environmental value depends on manufacture, longevity and actual use.
questions.explanation: The writer rejects simplistic symbols because life-cycle and actual-use conditions matter.

questions.q: What does the festival deposit-cup scenario reveal about storytelling?
choices: The same evidence can be edited into triumph or failure unless its limitations are examined.
The first summer's costs prove that the scheme should be stopped.
Missing returns always make a scheme unsuccessful.
A successful documentary must avoid technical details.
questions.explanation: An incomplete success can be framed selectively; the author proposes questioning design, measurement and costs.

questions.q: Why is the essay's desired audience not simply one that 'feels innocent'?
choices: A clean coastline is always a misleading image.
The better outcome is an audience able to interrogate explanations and missing causes.
Environmental documentaries should never include inspiring people.
The most urgent task is to make viewers feel guilty.
questions.explanation: The conclusion values analytical capacity more than temporary moral satisfaction.

questions.q: A school video shows pupils sorting rubbish but not where collected material goes. Which question would best extend its analysis?
choices: Which colour-coded bins are most attractive in a photograph?
Should the film include a more uplifting soundtrack?
How many pupil volunteers should appear smiling on screen?
What arrangements determine whether the sorted material is processed effectively?
questions.explanation: The author criticises the omission of municipal infrastructure in the waste-sorting sequence.

questions.q: Someone argues that individual habits are pointless until governments act. How would the author respond?
choices: Only government policy can determine whether a flask is reusable.
The strongest argument is that consumers should ignore public institutions.
Individual practices can also influence collective arrangements, so the separation is false.
Individual choices are sufficient to overcome every institutional obstacle.
questions.explanation: The writer rejects both a purely individualist narrative and an equally convenient absolution of consumers.

questions.q: A film reports fewer abandoned cups but unexpectedly high losses from a deposit scheme. What is the most responsible editorial choice?
choices: Use the results only to praise its organisers.
Explore design, measurement and who bears the costs before judging its success.
Remove all numbers so that the audience can feel inspired.
Call the scheme a total failure and abandon the discussion.
questions.explanation: The essay recommends examining mixed evidence rather than editing it into a simplistic triumph or disaster.
